DOCUMENT:
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432." -- Maintenance and licensing (£67,200) has been added to gross labour savings (£1,051,232) instead of subtracted. Correct net savings are £1,051,232 - £67,200 = £984,032, so payback on £1,344,000 is about 16.4 months, not 'about 14 months'.
2. [inconsistency] at: "Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:" -- The document elsewhere says the pilot ran in four stores and names them (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley); here the results are attributed to three pilot stores. The pilot store count contradicts itself.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit." -- Pilot stores were not randomly chosen: the document says they were selected because they had just been fully refurbished in early 2025 (and were larger). Refurbishment and store selection are obvious confounders for basket growth, so the comparison cannot show that self-checkout caused larger baskets.

REVIEW:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion Business Case

The case is well structured, and a ten-month pilot is stronger evidence than most capital papers have. It still has a **calculation error in the headline financials** and a **design flaw in the pilot** that undermines the basket-value claim and weakens several others. Both should be fixed before it goes to the Committee. Neither is likely to sink the case on its own.

## 1. The net savings figure is wrong

Section 5 says: *"After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432."*

That figure is the gross saving **plus** the maintenance cost, not minus it:

| | Paper | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Gross labour savings | £1,051,232 | £1,051,232 |
| Maintenance & licensing | £67,200 | −£67,200 |
| **Net annual savings** | **£1,118,432** | **£984,032** |
| Payback on £1,344,000 | ~14 months | **~16.4 months** |

As written, the net saving is *higher* than the gross saving, which a Committee member may spot quickly. Payback still clears the 24-month hurdle, so the recommendation survives. But the summary's "about £1.12 million" and "roughly 14 months" need correcting everywhere they appear. Since the summary says Finance has walked through the model, check whether the error is in the model itself or only in the paper.

The other arithmetic checks out: £14,500 × 6 × 14 = £1,218,000; £9,000 × 14 = £126,000; 95 × £15.20 × 52 = £75,088.

## 2. The pilot stores were not a fair comparison, so the basket-value claim doesn't hold

The pilot stores were chosen because they **"had been fully refurbished in early 2025"** and had spare floor space. The "other stores" column is therefore not a like-for-like control. Pilot stores got new self-checkout *and* a fresh refurbishment in the same period.

Refurbishments routinely lift basket value, through better layout, ranging and store appeal. So the +6% vs +2% gap cannot be attributed to self-checkout, and the paper's phrase *"which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit"* claims causation the data cannot support. The same confound partly affects the **satisfaction** result (+7 points). Queue times and staffed hours are much more plausibly driven by the kiosks.

Suggested fixes, in order of preference:
- Compare pilot stores against their own pre-refurbishment trend, or against other recently refurbished stores without kiosks, if any exist.
- Otherwise, describe basket value as "rose more in pilot stores, though this coincided with refurbishment" and drop it from the Recommendation's list of proven benefits.

Since the upside is already excluded from the financials, softening this costs the case nothing and protects its credibility.

## 3. The 95-hour saving may not transfer to the other 14 stores

- **Store size.** The saving is applied as a flat 95 hours per store, described as ~12% of "a typical store's" front-end hours. The rollout is "sequenced by store size", and the risks mention smaller rural stores, so sizes clearly vary. If pilot stores are larger than average, smaller stores will save fewer hours. Modelling the saving as a percentage of each store's actual front-end hours would be more defensible.
- **Floor space.** Pilot stores were picked *because* they could fit six kiosks without removing shelving. The other 14 were, by implication, not. They may need shelving removed (lost sales), fewer kiosks (lower savings), or more fit-out work than the flat £9,000 quote. The paper should say whether the vendor surveyed the remaining stores.

## 4. Are the labour savings cash savings?

In the pilot, hours were reduced partly by **redeploying colleagues into online order picking**. That is only a real saving if those picking hours would otherwise have been filled by new hires. If redeployment continues at scale, some of the £1.05m may move between budget lines rather than leave the cost base. A sentence on how much of the pilot reduction was turnover versus redeployment would close this gap.

The 38% turnover vs 12% hours comparison is reasonable at estate level. Turnover is uneven, though, and a small store with low turnover could still face a surplus. "We do not expect to need a consultation process" is fine. "No redundancy risk" (from your summary) is stronger than the evidence supports.

## 5. Smaller points

- **"Across the three pilot stores"** in Section 3 should be **four** (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme, Wexley).
- **Asset life.** No kiosk lifespan or replacement cycle is stated. Payback clears the hurdle, but a Committee may ask about total cost over five years.
- **Peak-time kiosk colleague.** Confirm the 95-hour figure is already net of this role in the pilot. If so, say so.
- **Shrink.** "Held flat" is a good result. A brief note on how it was measured (e.g. whether unknown loss at kiosks was tracked separately) would strengthen it, since this was the Committee's main concern.

## Summary of recommended changes

1. Correct net savings to **£984,032** and payback to **~16 months** throughout.
2. Fix "three pilot stores" → "four".
3. Acknowledge the refurbishment confound, and reframe basket value (and partly satisfaction) as encouraging but not attributable.
4. Scale labour savings to each store's size, or show that pilot stores are representative.
5. Confirm floor space and fit-out costs for the remaining 14 stores.
6. Clarify how much of the labour saving is a true cash reduction versus redeployment.

With these changes the case remains comfortably inside the hurdle. It will also be more robust to scrutiny, which matters more here than a slightly better headline number.
